sections.h: The return and the last years
sections.b: After Absalom's death David has to be shaken out of his grief by Joab (2 Samuel 19:1–8). His return to Jerusalem is a series of tests: he courts Judah, spares Shimei who cursed him, divides Mephibosheth's land without deciding who lied, and honors old Barzillai (2 Samuel 19). Sheba's revolt shows how fragile the union of Judah and Israel has become (2 Samuel 20). The book then closes with an appendix that steps back from the story: two national disasters for which a king is to blame (2 Samuel 21; 2 Samuel 24), lists and deeds of David's warriors, and two poems in David's voice, a long song of rescue (2 Samuel 22, also Psalm 18) and his "last words" about a just ruler and an everlasting covenant (2 Samuel 23:1–7). The last scene shows David confessing his sin, pleading for his people as "these sheep," and buying the threshing floor where the temple will stand.

common: David's song in 2 Samuel 22 and Psalm 18 is the same poem, handed down in two copies.
uncommon: Some historians read the Gibeonite executions (2 Samuel 21) as David's way of removing Saul's heirs under religious cover.

sections.h: Joab at the end of David's reign
sections.b: The last chapters show Joab at his most necessary and most dangerous. He alone tells the grieving king the truth (2 Samuel 19:5–7), yet David replaces him with Amasa (2 Samuel 19:13). Joab kills Amasa with a kiss and a sword (2 Samuel 20:9–10), wins the war against Sheba, and is back over the army in the next list of officials (2 Samuel 20:23). In the census story he is the voice of caution, and David overrules him (2 Samuel 24:3–4). Readers divide between those who see a loyal servant of the throne doing what the king could not, and those who see a killer who served himself. David's dying words to Solomon take the second view (1 Kings 2:5–6).

sections.h: At the Jordan, and spared again
sections.b: When David returns, Mephibosheth comes down unwashed, his feet and mustache untended since the day David fled, and says that Ziba tricked him and slandered him (2 Samuel 19:24–28). David answers by splitting the land between them, and Mephibosheth offers to let Ziba have it all because the king is safe (2 Samuel 19:29–30). The Talmud judged the split verdict harshly (Bavli Shabbat 56b). Later, when the Gibeonites demand seven of Saul's descendants, David spares Mephibosheth "because of the oath of the LORD between them, between David and Jonathan" (2 Samuel 21:7). Another Mephibosheth, Saul's son by Rizpah, is handed over (2 Samuel 21:8).

2 Samuel uses the word satan only for a human opponent: David tells the sons of Zeruiah that they have become his "adversary" by wanting Shimei dead (2 Samuel 19:22). The more famous link is 2 Samuel 24:1. Samuel says the LORD, in anger, stirred David up to count Israel; 1 Chronicles 21:1, retelling the story after the exile, says that Satan (or "an adversary") stirred him up. Many readers, especially Christian ones, say both are true, since God permits or uses an adversary (Job 1–2; 1 Kings 22:19–23). Sara Japhet suggests Chronicles meant an earthly adversary, and Peggy Day argues that satan in the Hebrew Bible always names one adversary or another, not a single figure called Satan. The Talmud explains 24:1 from David's own words to Saul about God "inciting" (1 Samuel 26:19): having called God an inciter, David was made to stumble over the half-shekel rule (Bavli Berakhot 62b). Many critical scholars see a development in which later writers assigned to a heavenly accuser what earlier writers said of God. James 1:13 is often brought in: God tempts no one.

common: 1 Chronicles 21:1 names Satan where 2 Samuel 24:1 names the LORD, and the two are usually harmonized by saying God allowed Satan to act.
uncommon: Some scholars read the Chronicler's satan as a human enemy, not a heavenly being.
Peggy Day argues that the Hebrew Bible has no single figure called Satan, only various adversaries, human and heavenly.

sections.h: The Three and the Thirty in 2 Samuel
sections.b: 2 Samuel ends its story of David with a roll of honor (2 Samuel 23:8–39). Three heroes come first, each with a short exploit: eight hundred slain at once, a hand frozen to a sword, a field of lentils held alone. Three warriors break through the Philistine lines to bring David water from Bethlehem, which he pours out to the LORD as if it were their blood. Abishai and Benaiah outrank the Thirty but do not reach the Three. Then come the Thirty, with names from Bethlehem, Tekoa and the hill country of Judah, a few foreigners, and last of all Uriah the Hittite. The four giant-killers of 2 Samuel 21:15–22 belong to the same tradition. The narrator credits the victories to the LORD (2 Samuel 23:10, 23:12).

claude.title: Claude's reading: water that cost blood
claude.body: My own reading: the narrator sets David's refusal to drink water his men risked their lives for (2 Samuel 23:15–17) near the end of a list that closes with Uriah (2 Samuel 23:39), the warrior whose life David spent to hide his sin. The two together show the best and worst of David's treatment of his men.

sections.h: Saul's crime and the Gibeonites' price
sections.b: A three-year famine in David's time is traced to Saul, who had tried to wipe out the Gibeonites in spite of Israel's oath to them (2 Samuel 21:1–2; Joshua 9:15–20). The Gibeonites refuse money and ask for seven of Saul's descendants, whom they put to death "before the LORD" at Gibeah (2 Samuel 21:4–9). The story shows how seriously the Bible takes an oath sworn in God's name, even to foreigners, and even generations later. It also raises hard questions, since the law forbids putting children to death for their fathers (Deuteronomy 24:16). Gibeon is also where Joab murders Amasa, by the great stone (2 Samuel 20:8–10).

Saul's body had been hung on the wall of Beth-shan and rescued by the men of Jabesh-gilead (1 Samuel 31:8–13). Years later, after Rizpah's long watch over her executed sons, David brings the bones of Saul and Jonathan from Jabesh and buries them with the seven in the tomb of Kish at Zela in Benjamin (2 Samuel 21:11–14). Saul ends where he began, in his father's land, and the narrator says that only then did God accept prayer for the land. The same chapter blames Saul's "zeal for Israel and Judah" for the famine (2 Samuel 21:1–2).

sections.h: The oath that saved Jonathan's son
sections.b: When seven of Saul's descendants are handed over to the Gibeonites, David spares Jonathan's son Mephibosheth "because of the oath of the LORD between them, between David and Jonathan son of Saul" (2 Samuel 21:7). Then David buries Jonathan's bones with Saul's in the family tomb (2 Samuel 21:12–14). The friendship sworn in 1 Samuel 20 is kept to the end of David's story.

2 Samuel 21:15–22 lists four Philistine champions "born to the Rapha" in Gath, all killed by David's men: Ishbi-benob, Saph, Goliath the Gittite and a man with six fingers on each hand and six toes on each foot. "The Rapha" is usually linked with the Rephaim, the tall old peoples of Deuteronomy, though some scholars think it names a warrior guild. The list closes the Bible's story of giants in the land, which began with the spies' fear (Numbers 13:33): under David the giants fall.

2 Samuel 21:19 says that "Elhanan son of Jaare-oregim the Bethlehemite struck down Goliath the Gittite, whose spear shaft was like a weaver's beam." 1 Chronicles 20:5 says Elhanan killed "Lahmi the brother of Goliath." The answers given: Chronicles has the better text and Samuel's was damaged (the Hebrew letters of "the Bethlehemite" and "Lahmi" are close); Elhanan was another name for David (the Targum, Rashi); there were two men named Goliath; or, as many critical scholars hold, Elhanan's deed was later told of David. Another "Elhanan son of Dodo, from Bethlehem" appears among the Thirty (2 Samuel 23:24).

In 2 Samuel 24 the LORD, angry with Israel, stirs David up to count Israel and Judah (1 Chronicles 21:1 says Satan). Joab objects, but the count takes nearly ten months and reports 800,000 fighting men in Israel and 500,000 in Judah; Chronicles gives 1,100,000 and 470,000 (1 Chronicles 21:5). David's conscience strikes him, and a plague kills seventy thousand. Why the count was wrong is never stated. Suggestions include the missing ransom of Exodus 30:12 (Josephus); pride in military strength; preparation for taxes and forced labor; the rabbinic rule that Israel may not be counted head by head, drawn from Hosea 1:10 (Hebrew 2:1), with Saul counting by tokens as the contrast (Bavli Yoma 22b); doubt of God's promise to make Israel as many as the stars (Genesis 15:5; 1 Chronicles 27:23); and Ramban's view that a count made with no need or command is wrong. Chronicles has Joab ask why it should "become guilt for Israel" (1 Chronicles 21:3). Josephus gives his own figures, 900,000 and 400,000. The numbers are widely judged too large for the period; some read 'elef as a unit rather than a thousand.

sections.b: The plague of 2 Samuel 24 stops at the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite, on the hill above David's city. The prophet Gad tells David to build an altar there. Araunah offers the floor, the oxen and the wooden threshing sledges for fuel, but David insists on paying, "I will not offer the LORD my God burnt offerings I got for free" (2 Samuel 24:24). Chronicles says the place became the site of Solomon's temple (1 Chronicles 22:1; 2 Chronicles 3:1). A working floor, open to the wind on a hilltop, becomes the place where God meets his people.

sections.h: The temple site bought by David
sections.b: 2 Samuel ends with David building an altar on the threshing floor of Araunah, where the plague stopped (2 Samuel 24:18–25). Samuel does not say what the place will become, but Chronicles does: "This is the house of the LORD God" (1 Chronicles 22:1), and Solomon's temple "stood on Mount Moriah... at the place David had made ready: the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite" (2 Chronicles 3:1). The Greek of Samuel (Codex Vaticanus and the Lucianic manuscripts) adds a last sentence that Solomon later enlarged the altar. The temple's site is bought at full price, like Abraham's burial cave (Genesis 23), and it is a place of mercy after judgment.

In the plague of 2 Samuel 24 an angel strikes the people from Dan to Beersheba and reaches out his hand toward Jerusalem, until the LORD tells him, "That's enough!" The angel of the LORD stands by Araunah's threshing floor (2 Samuel 24:16). Chronicles adds, and the Dead Sea scroll 4QSam-a seems to have had (the scroll's wording is largely reconstructed), that David saw him standing between earth and sky with a drawn sword over the city (1 Chronicles 21:16). The angel acts for God in judgment, as the "destroyer" did in Egypt (Exodus 12:23) and the angel who struck Assyria's army (2 Kings 19:35).

As the angel reaches toward Jerusalem, "the LORD regretted the harm" and ordered him to stop (2 Samuel 24:16). The verb is nicham, the same used of God's regret over Saul (1 Samuel 15:11, 15:35) and of his relenting after Moses' prayer (Exodus 32:14). Here God relents even before David's prayer in 24:17. The scene shows the pattern the Bible repeats: judgment is real, but God's compassion, which David trusted when he chose to fall into God's hand (2 Samuel 24:14), cuts it short.

The heading of Psalm 18 matches the opening of 2 Samuel 22 almost word for word: David spoke this song "on the day the LORD rescued him from the grip of all his enemies and from the grip of Saul" (2 Samuel 22:1). It is the one psalm whose title is also a sentence in a history book, so it shows how such headings could connect a psalm to David's life. The two copies of the poem differ in many small places; the chapter page on 2 Samuel 22 lists the main ones.

sections.h: The anointed in David's last poems
sections.b: David's song ends with God's loyal love "to his anointed, to David and his line for all time" (2 Samuel 22:51), and his last words call him "the God of Jacob's anointed one" and speak of a just ruler like morning light and an everlasting covenant (2 Samuel 23:1–5). In their setting these lines are about David's dynasty. The Targum reads the just ruler of 23:3 as the Messiah, and Christians read both poems as fulfilled in Jesus, son of David. Paul quotes the song's praise "among the nations" for the Gentiles who come to God through Christ (Romans 15:9).

sections.h: David calls the promise a covenant
sections.b: Nathan's promise of a lasting house for David (2 Samuel 7) does not use the word "covenant." David's last words do: God "has set up a covenant with me that lasts forever, laid out in every detail and guarded" (2 Samuel 23:5). Psalm 89 and Isaiah 55:3 use the same language. The covenant with David is the hinge for the later hope of a king from his line.

The Gibeonites "impale" (or "expose") seven of Saul's descendants on the hill before the LORD at the start of the barley harvest (2 Samuel 21:6–9). The bodies stay there, against the rule of Deuteronomy 21:22–23, until rain falls, while Rizpah guards them from birds and beasts. Only after David gathers the bones and buries them does God accept prayer for the land (2 Samuel 21:14). The same rare verb is used in Numbers 25:4.

The men of Jabesh-gilead had stolen the bodies of Saul and his sons from the square of Beth-shan and buried their bones under the tamarisk (1 Samuel 31:11–13). Years later David takes the bones from them and buries them in the family tomb of Kish in Benjamin (2 Samuel 21:12–14), completing the honor Jabesh began.

sections.h: Children for fathers? The Gibeonite case
sections.b: 2 Samuel 21 tests the Bible's teaching on guilt and punishment. Deuteronomy 24:16 says children must not die for their fathers' sins, yet seven of Saul's descendants die for Saul's attack on the Gibeonites. Readers explain it as the special case of an oath sworn in God's name and of a guilty "house" (2 Samuel 21:1), or read it as a political purge, or let the tension stand, noting that God's acceptance of prayer is reported only after the dead are buried (2 Samuel 21:14), though the rain had begun while the bodies still hung (2 Samuel 21:10). Rabbinic law later drew on another story in these chapters, Sheba's head thrown over the wall of Abel (2 Samuel 20:21–22), to decide when one person may be handed over to save many.

When David sees the angel striking the people, he asks God to turn his hand against him and his family instead of the people: "And these sheep, what did they do?" (2 Samuel 24:17). Like Moses after the golden calf (Exodus 32:32), the leader offers himself for those he has led into harm. Some ancient witnesses read "I the shepherd did wrong," which sharpens the picture.

Offered famine, flight or plague, David says, "Please, let us fall into the LORD's hand, for his compassion runs deep. Into a human hand, let me not fall" (2 Samuel 24:14). The book of Sirach turned the words into a proverb (Sirach 2:18). The story bears him out: the LORD stops the plague before it reaches Jerusalem (2 Samuel 24:16).

After Absalom's revolt the tribes quarrel over bringing David back. Israel claims "ten shares in the king" against Judah, and Judah answers that the king is its near kin (2 Samuel 19:41–43). Sheba then leads the north away with the cry, "We have no share in David" (2 Samuel 20:1), the same words the ten tribes use when they break from Rehoboam (1 Kings 12:16). The scene shows the fault line between Judah and the northern tribes that will split the kingdom.

David's last words call him ne'im zemirot Yisra'el (2 Samuel 23:1), famous in the King James Version as "the sweet psalmist of Israel." The phrase may mean Israel's sweet singer, the favorite of Israel's songs, or the favorite of Israel's Strong One. The first reading made David the patron of Israel's psalms; the second fits the songs women sang about him (1 Samuel 18:7). His long song of rescue (2 Samuel 22) is also Psalm 18.

sections.h: An oath to foreigners, and foreign heroes
sections.b: The Gibeonites "were not part of Israel" (2 Samuel 21:2), yet God holds Israel to the oath it swore them in Joshua's day, and Saul's zeal for Israel against them brings a famine. Among David's elite warriors are Zelek the Ammonite, Igal from Zobah in Aram, and Uriah the Hittite (2 Samuel 23:36–39), and his guard of Kerethites and Pelethites was foreign.

sections.h: David the prophet, Gad the visionary
sections.b: David's last words open like a prophet's oracle: "The declaration of David son of Jesse," and "The LORD's Spirit has spoken by me" (2 Samuel 23:1–2). The New Testament calls David a prophet on this basis (Acts 2:30). In the census story the prophet Gad, "David's visionary," brings God's word and then the instruction to build the altar (2 Samuel 24:11–19).

sections.h: Two copies of one song, and 4QSam-a
sections.b: 2 Samuel 22 and Psalm 18 are two copies of the same poem, handed down separately. Comparing them shows the ordinary ways hand copies drift apart: letters that look alike ("he was seen" and "he swooped," 2 Samuel 22:11 and Psalm 18:10), words dropped or added, and spelling. In 2 Samuel 24 the Dead Sea scroll 4QSam-a reportedly agrees with Chronicles against the traditional Hebrew text, for example in the scene of the angel with drawn sword (2 Samuel 24:16; 1 Chronicles 21:16). The scroll is broken there and much of its wording is restored from Chronicles, and scholars (Cross 2006; Himbaza 2010) differ over how much is preserved. Most conclude that the Chronicler used a Hebrew text of Samuel like the scroll's. In these chapters the Greek of Codex Vaticanus is a kaige revision toward the Hebrew, so the Lucianic manuscripts are the better witness to the Old Greek.

David had left ten concubines to keep the palace; Absalom took them in public (2 Samuel 16:21–22). On his return David provides for them but never goes to them again, and they live "widows for life" (2 Samuel 20:3). The women pay for what the men around them did, and the narrator gives them no voice.

David's song pictures near death as drowning and as a hunter's trap: "Death's breakers swept around me," and "The ropes of Sheol were wound around me" (2 Samuel 22:5–6). From that edge, God reaches down and draws him out of great waters (2 Samuel 22:17).
